scenes.name: Factory Records
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El sello de Tony Wilson, presentador de televisión educado en Cambridge y admirador de los situacionistas. Peter Saville le da una identidad visual de austeridad modernista (Bauhaus, De Stijl, constructivismo); el catálogo numera cualquier cosa (FAC 8, un temporizador menstrual de Linder; FAC 99, la factura del dentista de Rob Gretton). Sin contratos, «continua negación a la ganancia» y una firme voluntad federalista frente a Londres.

scenes.name: Joy Division
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: De Warsaw, rock pesado con influencias punk, a la desolación ballardiana: la originalidad crece a medida que las canciones se vuelven lentas y ralas, con el bajo de Peter Hook llevando la melodía, la guitarra de Bernard Sumner abriendo huecos, la batería de Stephen Morris rodeando un cráter y Ian Curtis recitando desde «un lugar solitario». Martin Hannett, productor de Factory, convierte el espacio en «control atmosférico» con delays digitales y grabaciones separadas: Unknown Pleasures (1979), con la portada del púlsar de Peter Saville, «Transmission», «Atmosphere». El coqueteo con la imaginería nazi, la epilepsia, los barbitúricos y un matrimonio roto desembocan en Closer, «estar dentro de la cabeza de Curtis», y en su suicidio en mayo de 1980. «Love Will Tear Us Apart» es su primer hit. Los supervivientes empiezan de cero como New Order.

xref.title: Discovery by Rob Gretton (1977)
xref.body: Rob Gretton, a Manchester punk scene figure and DJ, discovered the band formerly known as Warsaw (now trading as Joy Division) performing at approximately two in the morning as part of a talent showcase in 1977. A mere 20-minute set was enough to fully convince Gretton, who then launched a campaign to become their manager and ultimately secured the job.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rob Gretton's Peripheral Involvement (1977)
xref.body: In 1977, Rob Gretton was peripherally involved in the careers of two "pre-punk" bands, Slaughter and the Dogs and The Panik. This involvement predated his significant role in managing Joy Division and New Order.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rob Gretton's Peripheral Involvement (1977)
xref.body: Rob Gretton, a key figure in the Manchester punk scene, had peripheral involvement in the early careers of pre-punk bands like The Panik and Slaughter and the Dogs in 1977. This was before he took on management roles for more prominent groups.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Through Two Albums and Ian Curtis's Suicide (Until May 1980)
xref.body: Rob Gretton was the dedicated manager for Joy Division throughout the release of their two albums. His tenure with the band also encompassed the tragic event of singer Ian Curtis's suicide in May 1980.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Founding The Haçienda (1982)
xref.body: Rob Gretton was one of the key figures who conceptualized New Order opening their own nightclub in Manchester. This idea materialized into The Haçienda, which opened in 1982 in a former yacht showroom. While it became a central point of the Manchester music scene and a significant part of the 1980s DJ culture, it was a "complete and utter financial disaster" from its inception, costing New Order millions of pounds.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Embracing Dance Music Influence
xref.body: Rob Gretton was highly enthusiastic about dance music, particularly the sounds emerging from America in the early 1980s. He actively directed New Order's attention towards this genre, which had a profound effect on their evolving sound, integrating dance elements into their distinctive style.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin
xref.body: After Ian Curtis's death, surviving Joy Division members Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook, and Stephen Morris discussed their future. Encouraged by their progress as Joy Division, they decided to move forward under a new name. Their manager, Rob Gretton, suggested "New Order" after finding the phrase in a newspaper headline about mass killings in Pol Pot's Cambodia. "Their manager, my name Rob Greten, is the one who came up with it. He found the name in a newspaper headline about the mass killings in Pol Potts, Cambodia. The phrase was new order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

xref.title: Rebirth from Joy Division
xref.body: Following the suicide of singer Ian Curtis in May 1980, Joy Division was reborn as New Order, with Rob Gretton continuing as their manager. Gretton's involvement went beyond typical management, as he assisted the band with tasks like sorting song titles and even sang backup on some of their recordings.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rob Gretton Becomes Manager
xref.body: Joy Division's performance on Tony Wilson's TV show "So It Goes" made a strong impression on Rob Gretton, who subsequently became the band's manager. "When they made it to TV, their performance impressed another guy, Rob Gretton, the person who would become Joy Division's manager."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Signed by Rob Gretton to Factory Records
xref.body: Happy Mondays were among the bands that signed with Factory Records thanks to the efforts of manager Rob Gretton. Gretton's keen eye for talent helped populate the cool new indie label with significant acts from the Manchester scene.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Signing with Factory Records
xref.body: Under Rob Gretton's management, Joy Division signed with Factory Records, a "very cool, new indie label." Gretton's influence extended beyond Joy Division, as he also helped sign other bands, including Happy Mondays and OMD, to the label.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
